dok_rationale: Part (c) chooses a meaning for interest, matches counts or percentages to that meaning, and explains why unequal club totals can reverse the comparison.
stem: Two clubs asked the student council for money to run a Saturday session. Each club surveyed \emph{all} of its members: ``Would you attend a Saturday session?'' The table shows every response as a count.\par\smallskip At the council meeting, the \textbf{Robotics club} presented a \textbf{frequency table} (counts) and the \textbf{Chess club} presented a \textbf{relative-frequency table} (percents). Each club chose the table that made its case look best.
first_take: Which club has more interest in a Saturday session --- Chess or Robotics? One sentence and one number.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How many Robotics members said Yes?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the percent saying Yes in each club (nearest whole percent). Which is higher?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which club has more student interest? State whether you mean more people or a larger share, and use the matching numbers. Explain why the other measure favors the other club and what a reader needs to know to compare them fairly.

answers.b: Chess: $15/18\approx83\%$. Robotics: $27/45=60\%$. Chess has the higher percentage saying Yes.
answers.c: If interest means number of people, Robotics leads 27 to 15; if it means share of members, Chess leads about $83\%$ to $60\%$. Either interpretation earns credit when stated. The lead switches because Robotics has 45 members and Chess 18. Report the club totals with the percentages so readers can distinguish the number of interested students from the share. The full count table includes the totals; it does not hide them.

expectedElements.description: Chooses a club with a stated people-versus-share interpretation
Uses 27 versus 15 or 83 percent versus 60 percent consistently
Explains that different club totals reverse the lead and should accompany the percents

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: `Percents are always better' (or `counts are the real data') with no link to what the council asked
Cites 83\% without ever saying it is 15 people out of 18
Compares 27 Yes to 15 Yes without noting Robotics has 45 members to Chess's 18
Reports 27/45 as `27\%' --- treats a count as a percent

sentence_frames: By more interest, I mean \blank[1.5in], so I choose \blank[0.9in]: \blank[1.8in].
The other measure favors \blank[0.9in] because the club totals are \blank[1.4in]. Readers also need \blank[1.5in].

dok_rationale: Converting a frequency table to a relative-frequency table and checking that the percents add to 100 applies one known procedure across four categories with a self-check, no judgment between alternatives.
stem: Suppose 25 students in a class were asked their favorite lunch: Pizza 11, Tacos 8, Salad 4, Other 2. Make the relative-frequency table (nearest whole percent) and check that your percents add to $100\%$. Then write one sentence about the class that a reader could verify from your table.

answers.a: Pizza $11/25 = 44\%$, Tacos $32\%$, Salad $16\%$, Other $8\%$; sum $= 100\%$. Sentence names the variable and a checkable claim, e.g. ``Fewer than half the class (44\%) chose pizza'' or ``Pizza and tacos together make up 76\% of the class.''
